planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in lean, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; propagate vegetatively, since seedlings lose the dark stem color that defines this selection.

directions: Rosenkuppel is an RHS Award of Garden Merit ornamental oregano prized for near-black, wine-red stems and bracts that set off dangling clusters of rosy-purple flowers from midsummer into fall. The dusky purple cast carries into the young foliage before it matures to grey-green, giving the plant a moodier color palette than green-stemmed oregano cultivars. It is grown for bees and dried-flower structure rather than the kitchen, since flavor is secondary to ornamental impact in this selection. Cut the flowering stems back hard in late winter to keep the semi-woody base tidy and encourage a fresh flush the following season.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants after the last hard frost in lean, sharply drained, alkaline soil in full sun; site where winter wet drains away quickly, since crown rot rather than cold is the main threat to this species.

directions: Native to the Amanus Mountains of southern Turkey, this species forms a dense, low, wiry-stemmed mat of small aromatic leaves that stays only a few inches tall, in contrast to the papery hop-like bracts of Kent Beauty; instead it produces open, funnel-shaped, bright rose-pink flowers held just above the foliage from summer into fall. Its diminutive scale and tolerance for poor, gritty soil make it a natural for troughs, raised alpine beds, and rock garden crevices rather than the open border. Winter wet, not cold, is the main threat, so a raised, sharply drained planting site with alkaline soil is essential for it to persist. Trim lightly after the main flush of bloom to keep the mat compact and encourage rebloom.

common_name: Silver Queen Lemon Thyme (Silver-Variegated Lemon-Scented Thyme)

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Silver Queen does not come true from seed and must be propagated vegetatively to keep its silver-margined leaves.

directions: Silver Queen is the most widely grown variegated lemon thyme, forming a tidy, mounded plant of small dark-green leaves edged in soft silver-white, brighter and cooler in tone than the gold-leafed lemon thyme cultivars. It carries the same clean lemon fragrance and flavor as green lemon thyme, so it earns a spot at the herb-bed edge or rock garden for both a citrus-thyme seasoning and pale, frosted foliage color. Give it very well-drained, lean soil and full sun, since wet or overly rich ground quickly causes the woody base to rot and the variegation to fade. Shear lightly after the summer bloom to keep the mound dense and prevent woodiness.

common_name: Goldstream Creeping Thyme (Gold-and-Green Variegated Groundcover Thyme)

planting.note: Plant divisions or small plugs in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Goldstream spreads into a very low, tightly knit mat and roots readily wherever a stem touches soil.

directions: Goldstream is a prostrate creeping thyme whose small leaves are mottled and margined in yellow, green, and cream, giving the mat a warm, variegated glow that is distinct from the plain-green species. Mauve flowers appear in whorls along the trailing stems in summer, drawing bees, and the foliage releases a lemony thyme scent whenever it is brushed or lightly stepped on. Its extremely low, dense habit suits paving crevices, gravel paths, and between stepping stones, where the color and fragrance can be appreciated close to the ground. Divide congested mats in spring to renew vigor and to propagate new plants for filling in bare patches.

common_name: Albiflorus White Creeping Thyme (White-Flowered Groundcover Thyme)

planting.note: Plant divisions or small plugs in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; this white-flowered sport of creeping thyme is among the hardiest and lowest-growing thyme selections for a lawn-substitute planting.

directions: Albiflorus is a pure white-flowered form of creeping thyme that hugs the ground so tightly it is often grown as a flowering lawn substitute or stepping-stone filler in place of turf. In early summer the fine, light-green mat all but disappears beneath a smothering flush of small white blooms that draw bees in large numbers, a striking contrast to the pink and magenta tones of most other creeping thyme selections. It tolerates light foot traffic once established and is exceptionally cold hardy for a thyme, but still demands sharp drainage and lean soil, since it declines quickly in wet or heavy ground. Mow or shear lightly after flowering if a tidier, more turf-like appearance is wanted.

common_name: Peter Davis Thyme (Compact Lemon-Scented Pink-Flowered Alpine Thyme)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, sandy or gritty, lean, alkaline soil in full sun; this alpine thyme rots readily in wet or heavy ground.

directions: Peter Davis is a compact, mat-forming thyme with soft grey-green, lemon-scented foliage that holds a neat, cushiony habit rather than sprawling flat like common creeping thyme. Pale pink-mauve flowers cover the mound in late spring and summer, drawing bees, and the tidy, slightly domed shape suits rock gardens, alpine troughs, and border edging where a well-behaved, non-invasive thyme is wanted. It shares the same demand for lean, sharply drained, alkaline soil and full sun as other thymes, but is somewhat less cold-tolerant than common garden thyme and benefits from a gritty mulch and dry winter footing. Shear lightly after flowering to maintain the compact mound and encourage repeat bloom.

common_name: Hillary's Sweet Lemon Mint (Apple-Lime Hybrid Citrus Mint)

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings around the last frost date in consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade; this hybrid is sterile and must be propagated vegetatively to maintain its citrus character.

directions: Bred from apple mint and lime mint parentage, Hillary's Sweet Lemon combines a sweet, fruity apple-mint aroma with a bright citrus edge that leans more toward lemon than either parent, making it a favorite for iced tea, fruit salads, and desserts. Like other aggressive running mints it is best confined to a container or a buried bottomless pot to keep its spreading rhizomes from overtaking neighboring beds. Give it rich, consistently moist soil and afternoon shade in hot climates to keep the foliage lush and prevent scorching. Harvest and cut back regularly through the season to keep growth tender and to encourage a steady flush of fragrant new leaves.
